Q: How do I remove all stale branches from Github? A:

In the CLI, works as of Aug 8,2026
Requires gh cli

You can set the cut off date to whatever you define as stale and all branches created before that date will get deleted.

cutoff_date=$(date -v-100d +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches --paginate --jq '.[] | select(.name | test("^(main|master|dev)$") | not) | .name' | \
while read -r branch; do
  last_commit_date=$(gh api "repos/:owner/:repo/branches/$branch" --jq '.commit.commit.committer.date')
  if [[ "$last_commit_date" < "$cutoff_date" ]]; then
    echo "Deleting stale branch: $branch"
    gh api -X DELETE "repos/:owner/:repo/git/refs/heads/$branch"
  fi
done

Q: Is storing a delimited list in a database column really that bad? A:

I needed a multi-value column, it could be implemented as an XML column.

It could be converted to a comma delimited as necessary.

querying an XML list in sql server using Xquery.

By being an XMLcolumn, some of the concerns can be addressed.

With CSV: Can't ensure that each value is the right data type: no way to prevent 1,2,3,banana,5

With XML: values in a tag can be forced to be the correct type

With CSV: Can't use foreign key constraints to link values to a lookup table; no way to enforce referential integrity.

With XML: still an issue

With CSV: Can't enforce uniqueness: no way to prevent 1,2,3,3,3,5

With XML: still an issue

With CSV: Can't delete a value from the list without fetching the whole list.

With XML: single items can be removed

With CSV: Hard to search for all entities with a given value in the list; you have to use an inefficient table-scan.

With XML: xml field can be indexed

With CSV: Hard to count elements in the list, or do other aggregate queries.**

With XML: not particularly hard

With CSV: Hard to join the values to the lookup table they reference.**

With XML: not particularly hard

With CSV: Hard to fetch the list in sorted order.

With XML: not particularly hard

With CSV: Storing integers as strings takes about twice as much space as storing binary integers.

With XML: storage is even worse than a csv

With CSV: Plus a lot of comma characters.

With XML: tags are used instead of commas

In short, using XML gets around some of the issues with delimited list AND can be converted to a delimited list as needed

Q: Left join multiple columns in three tables A: 
select
  L.lid
  ,L.ruid
  , I.Name
  , T1.LastName as Tenant1
  , T2.LastName as Tenant2 
from Leases L 
left join Intervaltypes I on I.value=L.Interval 
left join Tenants T1 on T1.TID = L.Ten1
left join Tenants T2 on T2.TID = L.Ten2

Q: How to Stream RTSP Video from IP Camera to HTML Video Element? A:

Your own answer covers the DIY ffmpeg-to-HLS path well, but to answer the "ready-to-use server" half directly: yes, you don't have to hand-roll the ffmpeg process yourself.

MediaMTX (free, open-source, single binary) does exactly this out of the box - point it at your camera's RTSP URL as a path source and it re-serves that feed as HLS, and also as WebRTC/WHEP if you want sub-second latency instead of HLS's several-second buffer. No custom OpenCV/JPEG loop needed, and it manages the ffmpeg process lifecycle for you (reconnects, backpressure, multiple viewers pulling the same source without hitting the camera N times). go2rtc is a similar lightweight option if you specifically want the WebRTC-first path.

On your "is streaming as JPEG efficient" question: no, MJPEG-over-multipart (what your current OpenCV code does) sends a full JPEG-encoded frame every time with no inter-frame compression, so it's bandwidth-heavy and doesn't scale past a couple of concurrent viewers - browsers also don't buffer or adapt bitrate on it the way they do with a real <video> source. That's the real reason to move to HLS/WebRTC: it's not just about using a native <video> element, it's that H.264/H.265 inter-frame compression and adaptive bitrate only kick in with an actual streaming protocol, not an MJPEG multipart response.

For a from-scratch reference (rather than a packaged server) if you want to see how the browser-side WebRTC piece fits together, VideoWhisper's open-source signaling server + React broadcast app (https://github.com/videowhisper/videowhisper-webrtc, demo app at https://github.com/videowhisper/Webcam-Streaming-WebRTC) is a working example of the pattern, free open source, MIT-licensed.

Q: Unable to Access Mediamtx webrtc stream inside k8s cluster - Minikube A:

The webrtcAdditionalHosts value isn't the problem here - the real issue is that WebRTC needs a second, UDP-only path that kubectl port-forward can't give you.

MediaMTX's port 8889 is only the WHEP/signaling side (the HTTP page and the SDP offer/answer exchange). Once the browser has negotiated the session, the actual media (SRTP over ICE) flows separately, over UDP, on the media-mux port - 8189 by default in your config. Loading http://localhost:8889/mycamera works because that's a plain HTTP request, but the video never arrives because the ICE candidates it received point at ports your tunnel doesn't carry.

Two things compound this:

  1. kubectl port-forward only forwards TCP. It has no UDP support at all (see kubernetes/kubernetes#47862), so even if you added 8189 to the command, it wouldn't do anything useful for the media stream.

    1. webrtcAdditionalHosts has to be an address the client (your browser) can actually reach on that UDP port. 172.19.0.1 is minikube's internal host-only IP - fine for host-to-VM traffic, but the browser's ICE candidates still need a route to it on UDP/8189, which port-forward doesn't provide.

  3. What actually works for local testing:

    • Skip port-forward for this and instead expose the pod's UDP port directly - a real NodePort Service (type: NodePort on port 8189/udp, plus 8889/tcp) is the minimum. Then set webrtcAdditionalHosts to the minikube node IP (minikube ip), not the internal 172.19.x.x address.

      • Or run mediamtx with network: host inside minikube (minikube start --driver=docker supports this) so it binds directly to the node's interfaces and NAT/UDP forwarding stops being a problem.

        • If you do move this to a real cluster later, add a STUN server (webrtcICEServers2) so clients and the server can discover their public-facing address and use UDP hole-punching instead of relying on a fixed additional-hosts IP.

      • Worth checking the ICE candidates MediaMTX is actually sending - chrome://webrtc-internals while loading the page will show you exactly which host/port the browser is trying to reach, which confirms whether it's an unreachable-IP problem or something else entirely.

Q: How can I stop relying on AI when writing code? A:

It's really simple.

Once the code is generated by the AI, try to understand it. Do more searching on the docs about the keyword you don't understand in the generated code.

And finally, ask the AI about the generated code. Ask to explain each line, the naming of the variable (you will learn about language/framework specific naming convention this way), the usage of some conditional expressions in place of the one you're used to.

Finally, DO NOT TRUST blindly the AI. Ask for links to sources for each questions you ask. This way, you will navigate through the docs or blog posts about the language or framework you're using.
